content.text: Feature scaling isn't cosmetic, but it isn't universal either. Models that compare features through distances, penalties or gradient steps (k-nearest neighbors, SVMs, regularized linear models, anything trained by gradient descent) can change a lot: on scikit-learn's wine dataset, KNN goes from 0.663 to 0.961 accuracy. Tree-based models give exactly the same result. Know which kind you're using, and scale inside a pipeline.

A team prototypes "customers like you" recommendations with k-nearest neighbors on three columns: yearly spend in dollars, number of orders and average rating. The neighbors it returns are simply customers who spent about the same, whatever they ordered or rated. Someone suggests adding
. Someone else objects: "Scaling doesn't change the information. We tried it on the churn random forest and nothing moved." Both observations are true, and they're about different kinds of models.
Many developers treat feature scaling as optional, cosmetic preprocessing that never changes a model's results. There are good reasons it looks that way:

items.text: Scaling loses no information. Each column keeps its order and the relative spacing of its values, so it feels like changing units from meters to kilometers.
Tree-based models, a common first choice for tabular data, really are unaffected. Anyone who tried scaling with a random forest saw identical numbers.
as a ritual step without saying why, so it looks like hygiene, like formatting code.

content.text: The half-truth: scaling keeps the information
each column. But many models combine columns, adding them into distances, penalizing their weights together or stepping along all of them with one learning rate. Those comparisons depend on units.
, the usual choice, gives each feature a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Whether that matters depends on how the model uses the numbers.
scikit-learn's built-in wine dataset has 13 measurements per wine on very different scales. The script measures five models with 5-fold cross-validation, with and without scaling.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
print(X[:, 12].max(), X[:, 10].max())  # proline 1680.0, hue 1.71

# "Scaling is cosmetic": KNN on the raw columns
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
score = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(), X, y, cv=cv).mean()
print(f"KNN on raw features: {score:.3f}")  # 0.663

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for model in [KNeighborsClassifier(), SVC(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000),
              DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
              RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)]:
    raw = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv).mean()
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model)  # scaler fit per fold
    scaled = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv).mean()
    print(f"{type(model).__name__:<23} raw {raw:.3f}  scaled {scaled:.3f}")
# KNeighborsClassifier    raw 0.663  scaled 0.961
# SVC                     raw 0.657  scaled 0.983
# LogisticRegression      raw 0.955  scaled 0.983
# DecisionTreeClassifier  raw 0.927  scaled 0.927
# RandomForestClassifier  raw 0.972  scaled 0.972

content.text: Three models change, two don't move at all. The reason is in how each one uses the numbers.

KNN finds the closest training rows, and an SVM with its default RBF kernel also works from distances between rows. A distance adds up differences across all columns in their raw units. In the wine data, proline goes up to 1680 while hue tops out at 1.71, so a typical proline difference outweighs the full range of hue. scikit-learn's scaling example shows exactly this: without scaling, the neighbors are decided mostly by proline; after standardization, both features fall roughly between -3 and 3 and count about equally. That's KNN going from 0.663 to 0.961 and the SVM from 0.657 to 0.983. PCA suffers for a related reason: it looks for the directions of largest variance, and the same example shows proline dominating the first principal component when the data isn't scaled.

applies an L2 penalty by default, which shrinks all weights by the same rule. A feature measured in large units needs only a tiny weight, so it barely gets penalized, while small-unit features get squeezed. The scikit-learn preprocessing guide warns that such penalties may assume features have variance of the same order, and that a feature with a much larger variance can dominate the objective. Here, logistic regression moves from 0.955 to 0.983. With the default
, the unscaled version doesn't even finish: the
solver reports that it failed to converge after 100 iterations.
Gradient steps: one learning rate for every feature

to neural networks, use a single learning rate across all weights. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course lists what normalization buys you there: faster convergence, avoiding the "NaN trap" when values are very large, and letting the model learn appropriate weights for each feature.

A decision tree fitted on the wine data opens with the question "is proline at most 755?". Standardizing changes the threshold number, not which rows go left or right, so the same tree comes out. scikit-learn's example says tree-based models are (almost) unaffected by scaling, and the script agrees: the decision tree and the random forest print identical scores. Gradient-boosted trees such as
behave the same way, because they bin each feature by the order of its values.

blocks.title: Pick the scaler from the data

content.text: is the usual default. When a feature has many outliers, the scikit-learn guide suggests
, which uses statistics that outliers can't drag around. For power-law features, where most values are small and a few are huge, the Crash Course recommends log scaling first.

blocks.title: Fit on training data, ship with the model

content.text: scikit-learn's common pitfalls guide shows both failure modes. Fit the scaler on all the data before splitting and test information leaks into training. Forget to apply it at prediction time and the model sees a different feature space; in the guide's example, test error jumps from 0.90 to 62.80. A
that holds the scaler and the model avoids both.

Scaling gives every feature an equal voice. scikit-learn's scaling example notes that if the small-scale features were noise, scaling would boost their influence and increase overfitting. Compare both versions instead of assuming.
How to apply it in your project
Use the table above. If your model compares features through distances, penalties or gradient steps, scaling is part of the model, not cosmetics.

items.text: Scaling keeps the information within each column but changes how models compare columns.
Distance-based models, regularized linear models and gradient-trained models need it; on the wine data, KNN went from 0.663 to 0.961.
Tree-based models only use the order of values, so scaling leaves them unchanged.
Fit the scaler on training data inside a pipeline, and ship it with the model.
